title: Private credit faces 'real test' as cracks show
full_text:
The nation's $200 billion private credit sector is showing increasing signs of stress after some of its biggest firms limited redemptions on their portfolios, prompting the corporate regulator to warn that significant cracks were beginning to appear in the industry.
Australian Securities and Investments Commission chairwoman Sarah Court said private credit firms were facing their first "real test" after several private credit lenders were caught up in the collapse of Sydney property developer Bathla, which has more than $3.5 billion in debt.
"Unfortunately, what we're seeing at the moment - and it's early days, and no doubt more information will come out in the weeks and months to come - is the first significant cracks," said Court, at a lunch hosted by the Committee for Economic Development of Australia.
Her remarks came after MA Financial, which does not have exposure to Bathla, told investors on Tuesday that redemptions from its $2.3 billion secured property funds would be restricted to 1 per cent per month, amid an escalation in withdrawal requests. Investors have grown more anxious about the private credit industry's exposure to property development.
The collapse of Bathla, a major property developer in western Sydney, has engulfed some of the nation's largest private credit funds, such as CVS Lane, Centuria Bass, 360 Capital, Balmain Private and Credit Connect, amid a weakening property market and rising interest rates.
During its surveillance of 28 private credit funds last year, ASIC found poor practices including inconsistent and unclear reporting, opaque fee structures, weak governance, poorly managed conflicts of interest and bad valuation practices. It has called on the industry to lift its standards.
Morningstar analyst Thomas Dutka warned that "there is likely more pain down the track" for the sector.
"We've had a falling property market, rising interest rates as well and development costs. It's not surprising that there are signs of distress in that segment."
Earlier this month investors in another private credit fund, Merricks, which limited redemptions on its $1.2 billion flagship fund a year ago, were told redemption requests in June were cancelled due to the "fund's current liquidity position".
MA Financial joint chief executive Chris Wyke said his firm's decision to limit redemptions was a "proactive measure in response to the potential for increased redemption activity".
MA Financial is one of the country's largest private credit investment managers, and has $15 billion in funds under management, of which half is private credit.
Wyke conceded the private credit sector was experiencing challenges but said there was a "need for capital to fund the segments private credit currently finances".
"When large things occur, they have ripple effects throughout subsectors and markets, but the capital is required, and at the end of the day, an efficient and open market of capital will find a way to fill the void on price and terms."
The problems in Australian private credit come after a year in which some of the world's largest funds have suffered a crisis in confidence in private credit that led investors to pull billions of dollars of assets from the likes of Blue Owl, Blackstone and KKR.
The problems in the global private credit sector prompted JPMorgan Chase chief executive Jamie Dimon to remark that "when you see one cockroach, there are probably more".
The Australian private credit sector, which is heavily exposed to property development, is facing its moment of stress as souring property loans increase the risk of losses while investors are rushing to redeem capital from funds that have thus far delivered sound performance.
"People who don't really understand what they're invested in might start to tar everything with the same brush," said Joey Mouracadeh, senior director at investment advisory Stanford Brown. "As we've seen throughout history, a cause to act first and think later."
The Financial Services Council moved to lift standards across the industry, announcing on Wednesday its funds management and superannuation members would have to meet higher expectations on a range of issues including governance and accountability, valuations, liquidity and leverage, conflicts of interest, fee and income transparency and investor disclosure, from July next year.
Managers of private credit funds will need to use clear consistent terminology for arrears, defaults, impairments, watch list exposures, and loan-to-value ratios. They will be required to clearly explain when different approaches are used. They'll also need to disclose to investors deteriorating credit exposures, including impairments or negative revaluations.
"The FSC and our members have responded in good faith to ASIC's call for enhanced industry standards, to help address the legitimate concerns ASIC and the Reserve Bank of Australia have towards the private credit market," FSC chief executive Blake Briggs said.
ASIC commissioner Simone Constant said the next phase of ASIC's surveillance of retail and private credit funds was "well advanced", alongside multiple enforcement investigations, with findings and outcomes due in the coming months.
ASIC has repeatedly said that private credit funds have an important role to play in the economy. Constant said the FSC standards were "an important step towards lifting practices across a sector that has grown dramatically in size and breadth" and called on funds "to step up and adopt them with urgency". "The time is nigh for these standards when we look at recent market developments that unfortunately bear some marks of the concerns we have expressed over the past year and some of the areas we have had under close scrutiny," she added.
The Reserve Bank of Australia has started to explore where cracks might emerge and what might happen to the broader financial system if private credit were to suffer a serious widespread shock.
In its latest Financial Stability Review in March, the RBA said it was working with other regulators to monitor "for any material erosion in lending standards that would lead to a build-up of vulnerabilities in the sector and undermine future resilience". For now, it says private credit remains a small part of the overall financial system, representing less than 2 per cent of total loans, and does not create systemic risk.
MA Financial said it moved to limit withdrawals to protect investors.
"The temporary arrangements reflect the broader market, including uncertainty following proposed tax changes in the federal budget and recent publicity concerning other, unrelated private credit managers," Wyke said.
Shares in MA Financial slid 5 per cent to $6.23 while MA Credit Trust, the ASX-listed credit trust which has a 20 per cent exposure to the restricted fund, fell 2.8 per cent.
Morningstar's Dutka said private credit had proved popular with all kinds of investors from retail to institutional, but there was a "recalibration" taking place and more understood the potential delay in retrieving their money. "Private credit in Australia has not really been put through such a persistently high period of interest rates at such scale," Dutka said.
"There is now investor awareness about what could happen, and the illiquidity that lies under the surface. You are getting higher income, but that does come with a trade-off."
